original_value: Agricultural terraced landscapes, which are important historical heritage sites (e.g., UNESCO or Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS) sites) are under threat from increased soil degradation due to climate change and land abandonment. Remote sensing can assist in the assessment and monitoring of such cultural ecosystem services. However, due to the limitations imposed by rugged topography and the occurrence of vegetation, the application of a single high-resolution topography (HRT) technique is challenging in these particular agricultural environments. Therefore, data fusion of HRT techniques (terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) and aerial/terrestrial structure from motion (SfM)) was tested for the first time in this context (terraces), to the best of our knowledge, to overcome specific detection problems such as the complex topographic and landcover conditions of the terrace systems. SfM–TLS data fusion methodology was trialed in order to produce very high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) of two agricultural terrace areas, both characterized by the presence of vegetation that covers parts of the subvertical surfaces, complex morphology, and inaccessible areas. In the unreachable areas, it was necessary to find effective solutions to carry out HRT surveys; therefore, we tested the direct georeferencing (DG) method, exploiting onboard multifrequency GNSS receivers for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and postprocessing kinematic (PPK) data. The results showed that the fusion of data based on different methods and acquisition platforms is required to obtain accurate DTMs that reflect the real surface roughness of terrace systems without gaps in data. Moreover, in inaccessible or hazardous terrains, a combination of direct and indirect georeferencing was a useful solution to reduce the substantial inconvenience and cost of ground control point (GCP) placement. We show that in order to obtain a precise data fusion in these complex conditions, it is essential to utilize a complete and specific workflow. This workflow must incorporate all data merging issues and landcover condition problems, encompassing the survey planning step, the coregistration process, and the error analysis of the outputs. The high-resolution DTMs realized can provide a starting point for land degradation process assessment of these agriculture environments and supplies useful information to stakeholders for better management and protection of such important heritage landscapes.

result.paraphrase: Agricultural terraced landscapes, which are important historical heritage sites such as UNESCO or Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS) sites, are threatened by climate-change-driven soil degradation and land abandonment. Remote sensing can help assess and monitor these cultural ecosystem services. However, rugged topography and vegetation make it difficult to use a single high-resolution topography (HRT) technique in these agricultural settings. For this reason, data fusion of HRT methods—terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) and aerial/terrestrial structure from motion (SfM)—was tested here for the first time in terrace environments, to our knowledge, to address detection challenges posed by the complex topography and land-cover conditions of terrace systems. The SfM–TLS fusion approach was trialed to generate very high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) for two agricultural terrace areas characterized by vegetation covering parts of the subvertical surfaces, complex morphology, and inaccessible zones. In unreachable areas, effective solutions were needed for HRT surveys, so we tested direct georeferencing (DG), using onboard multifrequency GNSS receivers on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) together with postprocessing kinematic (PPK) data. The results indicated that combining data from different methods and acquisition platforms is necessary to produce accurate DTMs that capture the true surface roughness of terrace systems without data gaps. In addition, for inaccessible or hazardous terrain, using both direct and indirect georeferencing proved useful for reducing the major inconvenience and expense of placing ground control points (GCPs). We demonstrate that achieving precise data fusion under these complex conditions requires a complete, task-specific workflow that addresses all data-merging and land-cover issues, including survey planning, coregistration, and output error analysis. The resulting high-resolution DTMs can serve as a starting point for assessing land-degradation processes in these agricultural environments and provide stakeholders with useful information for improved management and protection of these important heritage landscapes.
